736.title: The learned man of Benares
736.hook: tradition says a Benares pandit tested Nanak with learning and heard him sing the Oankar
736.howItsDone: The Oankar, which tradition links to Guru Nanak's meeting with a pandit, is part of the Guru Granth Sahib and is sung and studied by Sikhs, verse by verse through the letters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kurukshetra, and your line, kindly, question it. Which habit did you ask, gently, what it's for? Day seven hundred thirty-six.

A child at a kitchen table, tracing the alphabet with a fat pencil. A says apple. B says ball. Every letter is a door to one small thing. Somewhere along the way, the letters stop being seen at all. They become the furniture of reading. Today's sakhi takes us to Benares, a city of scholars on the river Ganges, where a learned man meets a traveler and they end up talking about letters, of all things. Not apple and ball. Something much bigger. Today: Oankar.
screen: `A IS FOR APPLE.` → `LETTERS BECOME FURNITURE.` → `A CITY OF SCHOLARS.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana arrive in Benares and sit by the river. A pandit, a learned man of the city, notices this traveler with no sacred marks, no scholar's books, and a musician at his side. Some tellings give him a name, Chatur Das. He comes to test the Guru. What do you know? What have you studied? What can you recite? Tradition says Nanak answered by singing. And the hymn he sang, tradition says, was the Oankar, a long composition now in the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's the clever thing about it. A pandit taught with letters: students wrote them on a wooden slate, one by one. The Oankar takes the pandit's own tools and turns them. Its verses move through the letters, and each letter becomes a door to the One. It opens with Oankar itself, the One, from whom even Brahma, the creator god of the pandit's own books, came into being. And then letter by letter, it speaks of God, of the mind, of the false and the true, of what learning is for. So the Guru doesn't throw learning away. He takes the alphabet a scholar loves and shows him where every letter points. In the tellings, the pandit listens, and bows. Notice who bows. Not a fool, but a learned man. And not because he lost an argument. Because he heard his own learning sung back to him, deeper than he'd been reading it. Sikh tradition honors study; the Gurus wrote, collected and taught. Learning bows, in this story, when it remembers what it's about.
screen: `A PANDIT TESTS THE TRAVELER.` · `THE GURU SINGS THE OANKAR.` · `EACH LETTER A DOOR TO THE ONE.` · `THE LEARNED MAN BOWS.` · then, large: `LEARNING BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one letter's meaning. Pick a letter. Any letter, in any alphabet you know. Settle and breathe. Say its sound quietly. Then let it lead you to one word that matters to you: a name, a place, a quality you want more of. Hold that word for the rest of the sit. If you'd like, look up one letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet later today and learn its shape. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and notice the letters in it. The bell holds the time.
Oankar, the hymn tradition says Nanak sang for the learned pandit of Benares who tested him, where every letter points to the One.
Your line: learning bows. Today, take one thing you know well and ask it what it's really about. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: Farid's successor
737.hook: tradition says Nanak met Farid's spiritual heir at Pakpattan and gathered Farid's verses
737.howItsDone: Sheikh Farid's couplets are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are read and sung in gurdwaras like the rest of Gurbani, and Sikhs retell the sakhi of Nanak at Pakpattan as part of how those verses came to be kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oankar, who came to test Nanak and stayed to listen. Your line was learning bows. Did you learn the meaning of one letter? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

A box of letters turns up in an attic after a grandparent dies. Nobody else knew they existed. Someone has to decide: keep them, copy them, or let them go out with the old furniture. Words get lost that way, one attic at a time. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a meeting where a set of old verses could have been lost, and weren't. It happens in a river town in the Punjab, at the shrine of a Sufi poet who had died long before. Today: Farid's successor.
screen: `A BOX OF LETTERS IN AN ATTIC.` → `KEEP THEM, OR LET THEM GO?` → `A SUFI SHRINE BY THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: We met Sheikh Farid back in year one: the Sufi of Pakpattan, whose couplets in the Granth are in Punjabi, the language of the fields. Today is about how his words traveled. Tradition says that on his journeys Guru Nanak came to Pakpattan and met the man then sitting in Farid's seat, his spiritual heir, a Sufi teacher in Farid's line. The janamsakhis picture two seekers talking, not a contest. They ask each other about God, about love, about how a person should live. And in the telling, the Sufi recites Farid's verses, and Nanak listens closely enough to carry them away. Tradition says that is how Farid's couplets came into the Guru's keeping, passed along the line of Gurus until they were written into the Granth. Historians discuss the details; the story is the one Sikhs tell. Here is one couplet, from Ang 1378, in plain paraphrase: Farid, if you are clever and fine of mind, don't write black marks against anyone else. Bow your head and look inside your own collar. Notice what that does. It turns the sharp mind around. The cleverness that would make a list of other people's faults is sent to look at its owner instead. And notice something else about the page. Among Farid's couplets in the Granth sit couplets by the Gurus themselves, answering him, adding a line, gently turning a thought. A Sufi and the Gurus, side by side on one page, in conversation. The verses weren't just stored. They were kept alive by being talked with.
screen: `FARID WROTE IN PUNJABI.` · `NANAK MEETS FARID'S HEIR.` · `LOOK INSIDE YOUR OWN COLLAR.` · `THE GURUS ANSWER FARID ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `THE VERSES KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse of Farid. Take today's couplet. Say it slowly to yourself: don't write black marks against anyone else; look inside your own collar. Then use the sit. Let one person you've been quietly keeping a list on come to mind. You don't need to excuse them. Just set the list down for two minutes, and turn and look at your own collar instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Farid's successor. The Sufi in Farid's seat at Pakpattan who, in the story, shared Farid's verses with Nanak, so they could be kept.
Your line: the verses kept. Today, copy out one line someone older gave you, a saying, a recipe, a joke, before it's lost. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

738.title: The king of the island
738.hook: tradition places Nanak at the court of Raja Shivnabh in the south, who waited years to meet him
738.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the sakhi of Raja Shivnabh as a story of longing and recognition, and gurdwaras connected with Guru Nanak's southern journey keep his memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid's successor, and a Sufi's couplets passed on at Pakpattan. Your line was the verses kept. Whose words did you copy down before they were lost? Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

A trader steps off a boat onto an island in the far south, with goods to sell and habits people there notice. On a day when the town keeps a fast, he doesn't. He gets up before dawn, sings, and then goes to work. Word reaches the palace, and the king sends for him. Who taught you to live like this? The trader gives a name, a teacher far away in the north. And the king, the story says, decides he will not rest until that teacher stands in his court. Today: Raja Shivnabh.
screen: `A TRADER STEPS OFF A BOAT.` → `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO LIVE LIKE THIS?` → `THE KING DECIDES TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: The janamsakhis call him Raja Shivnabh, a king on an island in the south. The trader is remembered as Bhai Mansukh, a Sikh of Guru Nanak. Tradition says the king asked him how he would know the Guru if he came, and Mansukh said, roughly, you'll know when your heart goes quiet. So the king waited. Not a week. In the telling, years. And waiting made him a target. Word got out that the king longed for a holy man, so pretenders started to arrive, dressed for the part, full of fine speeches, hands out for gifts. The king received every one. None of them was the one. Then, the story goes, a traveler sat down quietly in a garden outside the city, with a companion and a rabab, and began to sing. No announcement. When the king came, he tested him, sending dancers and gifts to see whether this man too could be bought or flattered. Nanak was not moved. And the king's heart, at last, went quiet. What does the story know about waiting? That it was real: Shivnabh didn't settle for the nearest impressive person. That the imitations came first, because a long wait draws them, and part of waiting well is telling the loud thing from the true thing. That the real one arrived plainly, and sat in a garden, not on a throne. And it knows something about the trader. One person living honestly on an island was the whole reason a king started looking.
screen: `A SIKH TRADER ON THE ISLAND.` · `THE KING WAITS, AND IMITATORS COME.` · `A SINGER SITS IN A GARDEN.` · `THE KING'S HEART GOES QUIET.` · then, large: `WORTH THE WAIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait patiently for one thing. Choose something you're waiting on right now. A reply. A result. A person to change. A season of life to end. Name it once, quietly. Then, for the sit, don't reach for the phone and don't rehearse what happens next. Just wait, the way the king waited, with the door open. Notice the urge to grab the nearest substitute, and let it pass. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Raja Shivnabh, who in the story waited for Nanak, turned away every imitation, and knew the true one when his heart went quiet.
Your line: worth the wait. Today, when something is slow, say the line once instead of settling for the first quick thing on offer. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

739.title: Mardana's last song
739.hook: tradition says when Mardana died, Nanak asked his son Shahzada to carry on playing
739.tomorrow: The boy who feared the fire
739.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana as Guru Nanak's companion and rabab player, and the rabab and the rababi tradition of kirtan are honored in Sikh music.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raja Shivnabh, who waited for Nanak and turned away every imitation. Your line was worth the wait. What did you wait for without grabbing a substitute? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

A guitar case sits by the door after the funeral. Nobody wants to open it. Everybody knows what's inside: the strings he tuned, the pick still tucked under them. Somebody, someday, has to decide what happens to it. All along this path, when Nanak sang, a rabab played beside him, in the hands of Mardana, the Muslim musician who walked the long roads with him. In the sakhis, he was there at the strange cities, the hunger, the bitter fruit. Today the music changes hands. Rabab.
screen: `A GUITAR CASE BY THE DOOR.` → `MARDANA'S RABAB.` → `THE MUSIC CHANGES HANDS.`

segments.voice: Tellings disagree about where Mardana died. Some place it on the road, far to the west; some at Kartarpur, near the end of Nanak's travels. What they share is the shape. Tradition says that as Mardana grew weak, Nanak sat with him and asked what he wished for his body, whether he wanted a tomb raised over him, as was done for honored men. And Mardana, the story goes, said no. Why trap me in a tomb of stone, when you've freed me from the tomb of the body? In some tellings, Nanak and his Sikhs then sang hymns for him, and Nanak told the family not to wail but to sing the Lord's praise. Then comes the turn. Tradition says Nanak called Mardana's son, Shahzada, and asked him to take up the rabab and keep playing. Look at what this ending keeps. A friendship that never asked Mardana to stop being who he was: a Muslim musician and a Guru, side by side to the end. Look, too, at what doesn't get built. No monument. The memorial is the music. And the sound didn't stop with one man. Sikh tradition remembers rababis, rabab players descended from Mardana, playing kirtan in the courts of later Gurus. Then there's the son. Grief can make the music stop. In this story, the comfort Nanak gives is a job: pick it up, and play.
screen: `TELLINGS DIFFER ON WHERE.` · `NO TOMB OF STONE.` · `SHAHZADA TAKES THE RABAB.` · `THE MEMORIAL IS THE MUSIC.` · then, large: `KEEP PLAYING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a musician. Use the sit to choose one. A singer who carried you through a hard year. The person who leads the hymns where you worship. A grandparent who hummed while cooking. A kid down the street learning trumpet badly and bravely. Let the sound come back to you for a moment. Then decide how you'll say thank you today: a message, a coin in a case, a word after the service. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Rabab, the instrument Mardana played to the end of his life, when, tradition says, he refused a tomb and Nanak gave it to his son Shahzada.
Your line: keep playing. Today, pick back up one small good thing someone you loved used to do, and do it once. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 739 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOY WHO FEARED THE FIRE.`

740.title: The boy who feared the fire
740.hook: tradition says a boy told Nanak small sticks catch fire first, so death takes the young too; he became Baba Buddha
740.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Baba Buddha as a revered elder of the early community, and the story of the boy and the kindling is a sakhi told to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rabab, and a rabab handed to his son. Your line was keep playing. Which small good thing did you pick back up? Day seven hundred forty.

Kids ask the questions adults have learned to step around. Where do people go when they die? Will you die? Will I? Sometimes the grown-ups change the subject, or say not for a long, long time. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a boy who asked that question and didn't accept the easy answer, because he'd already worked out the hard one himself, watching his mother at the stove. Nanak, the story says, was so struck that he gave the boy a new name. Today: Baba Buddha.
screen: `WILL I DIE TOO?` → `THE EASY ANSWER.` → `A BOY WHO WORKED IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here is the story as tradition tells it. Nanak was staying near a village, and a boy who grazed the village cattle began coming to him every day, bringing milk, sitting nearby, listening. One day Nanak asked him why a boy his age spent his time with holy talk instead of play. And the boy answered with something he'd seen at home. When my mother lights the fire, he said, she puts in the small sticks first, and they catch before the big logs. So who can say death will wait for the old? It takes the young too. Nanak, the story goes, said: you are young in years, but you speak like an old man. And he called him Buddha: old one. The boy grew up to be Baba Buddha, the revered elder Sikhs remember serving the Gurus who came after Nanak. Where did the boy's wisdom come from? Not a book. A kitchen fire, and a habit of noticing. And he wasn't morbid. His fear didn't make him hide; it made him come and sit and listen, every day. Then there's the name. Being called old, in this story, is high praise, not a joke about wrinkles. And the grown-up in the story didn't brush him off. A Guru took a cowherd boy's question seriously enough to answer it with a name he would carry for life.
screen: `A COWHERD BOY BRINGS MILK.` · `SMALL STICKS CATCH FIRST.` · `YOU SPEAK LIKE AN OLD MAN.` · `THE BOY BECOMES BABA BUDDHA.` · then, large: `WISE WHEN YOUNG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think seriously for a minute. Not gloomily. Seriously. Let the boy's question sit with you: no one is promised a long life. Then, gently, ask what you'd want today to hold if it were the measure. One person you'd want to have spoken to. One thing you'd want to have finished, or forgiven. Hold that for the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Baba Buddha, the name Nanak gave the young cowherd who, in the story, saw small sticks catch first and spoke of death taking the young, not only the old.
Your line: wise when young. Today, when a young person says something wise, stop and tell them so. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: Settle here, scatter there
741.hook: tradition says Nanak blessed a rude village to stay put and a kind one to scatter, so goodness would spread
741.howItsDone: Sikhs tell this sakhi of the two villages to explain that goodness is meant to travel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baba Buddha, and the name Baba Buddha. Your line was wise when young. Did you catch a young person saying something wise, and tell them? Day seven hundred forty-one.

Two travelers come into a village at dusk, dusty and hungry. Doors close as they pass. Someone laughs at their clothes. Someone tells them to move along. Nobody offers water. In the morning they leave, and one of them, Nanak, turns and gives the village a blessing: may you stay here, settled, just as you are. The other, Mardana, says nothing. He's tired. A day later, a different village. Here they are fed, given a place to sleep, sent off with bread for the road. And as they leave, the blessing is: may you be scattered. Mardana stops walking. Today: settle here.
screen: `DOORS CLOSE AT DUSK.` → `MAY YOU STAY SETTLED.` → `KINDNESS, AND THEN: MAY YOU SCATTER.`

segments.voice: In the sakhi, Mardana can't hold it in. The rude village gets to stay comfortable, and the good village gets broken up? That's backward. And tradition gives Nanak's answer, roughly: if the unkind people stay where they are, their unkindness stays there with them. If the kind people scatter, their kindness goes everywhere they go. Wherever they settle, a new village learns how to welcome a stranger. This is a sakhi that surprises on purpose. It sounds like a curse and a blessing swapped, and the surprise is the teaching. Mardana says out loud what a listener might be thinking. It also changes what a blessing is for. Here, a blessing isn't a reward handed to the deserving to keep. It's a seed, and seeds are meant to be carried. Now look at scattering from the side of the people scattered. Leaving home is hard. The story doesn't pretend it isn't. It says that even a hard move can carry something good into a new place. And the rude village? Nanak doesn't curse it. He leaves it in peace, as it is. The story isn't about punishing anyone. It's about where goodness goes: a meal, a place to sleep, bread for the road, carried out of one village and set down in many.
screen: `MARDANA: THAT'S BACKWARD.` · `UNKINDNESS STAYS WHERE IT IS.` · `A BLESSING IS A SEED.` · `NOBODY IS CURSED.` · then, large: `GOODNESS SPREADS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry one kindness elsewhere. Use the sit to find it. Think of a kindness someone showed you, the kind you were glad of. Maybe a neighbor who brought food, a teacher who stayed late, a stranger who held a door in the rain. Now think of a different place you'll be today, where nobody knows that kindness exists: an office, a bus, a family chat. Decide how you'll do it there, in your own way. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Settle here. The blessing Nanak gave the unkind village in the sakhi, while the kind one was blessed to scatter, so its goodness would travel.
Your line: goodness spreads. Today, take one kindness out of the place where you got it, and do it somewhere new. Day seven hundred forty-one.

742.title: Bhumia's promises
742.hook: tradition says a robber promised Nanak never to lie, harm the poor or betray a host, and the promises changed him
742.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the sakhi of Bhumia the robber as a story about honest earning and keeping one's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, settle here, scatter there, and two villages with backward-sounding blessings. Your line was goodness spreads. Where did you carry a kindness somewhere new? Day seven hundred forty-two.

A rich man keeps an open kitchen. Holy men passing through his district eat well at his table, and they leave praising his generosity. There's just one thing nobody says aloud. The money for the feast comes from robbery. Bhumia, the sakhis call him, a landholder who raids by night and feeds saints by day. Then Nanak comes through, and sits at the table, and doesn't eat. Bhumia wants to know why. Today: Bhumia's promises.
screen: `AN OPEN KITCHEN.` → `PAID FOR BY ROBBERY.` → `NANAK DOESN'T EAT.`

segments.voice: In the sakhi, Nanak tells him plainly: food bought with stolen money isn't something he'll eat. Bhumia says he can't give up robbing; it's who he is. So Nanak, the story goes, asks for something smaller. Three promises. Never tell a lie. Never harm the poor. Never betray anyone whose salt you have eaten, whose food you've shared. Bhumia agrees. Those sound easy. That night he sets out to rob the king's palace, dressed so finely the guards take him for a nobleman. One asks who he is, and he remembers promise one. A thief, he says. The guard laughs and waves him in. Inside, he gathers treasure, and in the dark he tastes something from a dish. Salt. The king's salt. Promise three. He sets the treasure down and leaves with nothing. In the morning the palace finds things moved and nothing taken. The king's men find Bhumia, and asked straight out, he tells the truth, because of promise one. Tellings differ on what the king did next, but they agree the robber was a changed man, and that he found Nanak again and gave up robbery for good. Notice the size of what was asked. Nanak didn't demand a whole new life at once. He asked for three small promises. And notice how they worked. They didn't change Bhumia's mind first. They changed what he could do, one night at a time, until there was no room left for the old life.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one promise. Not a big one. Something like Bhumia's: small enough to say yes to tonight, real enough to matter. I won't lie about this one thing. I won't snap at the person who serves my coffee. I'll keep the confidence a friend gave me. Use the sit to choose it, word it plainly, and say it once, quietly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Bhumia's promises. Never lie, never harm the poor, never betray one whose salt you've eaten: the three small promises that, in the sakhi, turned a robber around.

Your line: promises change us. That ends a week of sakhis: the learned man of Benares, Farid's successor, the king of the island, Mardana's last song, the boy who feared the fire, two villages, and Bhumia. Today, keep your one promise. Day seven hundred forty-two.
